'''Decipher and the ''Star Wars'' CCG Lucasfilm license''' covers [[Decipher]]'s license to publish SWCCG, its pitch to keep it, and the license's end on 31 December 2001. Lucasfilm then gave the card-game rights to Wizards of the Coast, and Decipher handed SWCCG to the volunteer [[Players Committee]].

== The license ==

Decipher was meeting Lucasfilm at Skywalker Ranch as a licensee by November 1994, while developing its ''Star Wars'' game.<ref name="vapilot1994" /> [[Premiere Limited|Premiere]] shipped in December 1995. In 1998 Lucasfilm renewed the license and extended it to ''The Phantom Menace''.<ref name="wp-swccg" /><ref name="duelist25" />

== The pitch to keep the license ==

[[File:Skywalker-Ranch-presentation-card-encyc.png|thumb|right|300px|•Skywalker Ranch, promotional card made to show Lucasfilm.<ref name="encyc3" /><ref name="bisco20261021" />]]

In July 2000 Decipher pitched Lucasfilm executives on its plans for the license.<ref name="pres2000" /> It proposed marketing programs (sweepstakes for walk-on roles, set visits and Ranch visits, World Championship prizes, George Lucas signature cards, in-theater promotions, mall tours and fast-food premiums), a digital ''Star Wars'' CCG, and a backward-compatible [[SWCCG 2nd Edition]] for 2001. It asked Lucasfilm to treat card games as a core category, give earlier access to film material, ease channel restrictions and avoid over-licensing. Decipher pointed to roughly a quarter of a billion dollars that customers had spent on Decipher's ''Star Wars'' games. Lucasfilm approved none of it.<ref name="pres2000" />

Decipher also made a special promotional card to show Lucasfilm, the Location '''[[Playtest cards#Skywalker Ranch|•Skywalker Ranch]]'''. It is not a playtest card.<ref name="bisco20261021" /> Its game text reads "If you occupy, Decipher gets the CCG license here." Its copyright line is dated 2000.<ref name="encyc3" />

After the loss, Chairman [[Warren Holland]] said Decipher had offered Lucasfilm more money than for any previous license. He blamed the influence of Hasbro and Wizards of the Coast and a push toward younger, ''Pokémon''-style games. He did not disclose the terms of a settlement with Lucasfilm.<ref name="icv2-2002" /><ref name="tfn2001" />

== End of the license ==

Decipher announced on 28 December 2001 that Lucasfilm would not extend the license.<ref name="ann122801" /><ref name="tfn2001" /> Wizards of the Coast received an exclusive multi-year worldwide trading-card license and planned a new game with ''Episode II'' content for 2002.<ref name="icv2-2002" />

[[Game Players Network]] posted a Lucasfilm form letter on 8 January 2002 as "Lucasfilm Comments on Star Wars License". [[Howard Roffman]], President of Lucas Licensing, wrote that the decision was his responsibility. He wrote that Lucasfilm had begun two years earlier to decide what to do when the Decipher license expired at the end of 2001, had heard presentations from Decipher and Wizards of the Coast, and had talked to players and retailers. After nine months, he wrote, Lucasfilm concluded that Wizards had a better vision for the long-term future of ''Star Wars'': an improved game that could broaden the player base with a multi-layered experience in a single game (as opposed to multiple games for different audiences), designed by [[Richard Garfield]], and an improved organized play system.<ref name="gpn-roffman" /> He wrote that Wizards had been working on the successor for more than a year and asked readers to wait for the April launch. He wrote that Decipher would not produce any new ''Star Wars'' products, that Lucasfilm expected the existing games to go on, and that Decipher had committed to continue those games for as long as the player community wanted to play them.<ref name="gpn-roffman" />

<blockquote>
Thank you for writing to express your feelings about our Star Wars CCG decision. That decision was my responsibility, and I would like you to have a better understanding of how the decision was made.

I have worked for Lucasfilm for 21 years. For the last 16 years, I have been in charge of all of our merchandising. I have stayed with the company this long because I love Star Wars, and I know that millions of people throughout the world share that love. Not every decision I have made has been right, but I can tell you that every product decision is motivated first and foremost by whether it will result in a better experience for the fans of Star Wars.

Two years ago we began a painstaking process of figuring out what to do with the Star Wars CCG when the Decipher license expired at the end of 2001. We heard extensive presentations from Decipher and Wizards of the Coast, and we talked to many, many players and retailers. We faced a very difficult decision because Decipher had done a great job with the Star Wars CCG and is a terrific company with many wonderful and talented people. Wizards is also a great company and holds a very special position as the originator of the CCG format and the creator of Magic: The Gathering. We were honored that they were interested in Star Wars and listened very carefully to what they as well as Decipher and the fans had to say. After nine months of an exhaustive process, we came to the conclusion that Wizards had a better vision for the long-term future of Star Wars. That vision encompassed an improved game that could broaden the player base by offering a multi-layered experience within a single game (as opposed to multiple games for different audiences) and would be designed by Richard Garfield himself, and an improved organized play system that would support players better than ever before.

This was a very difficult decision given the strengths of both companies, our long history with Decipher, and the considerable investment that many players had already made in the existing games. In the end, we felt we had to do what was right for the fans in the long run, knowing that our decision would not be well received by everyone. Sometimes change is hard to accept, but our experience has been that change can be a good thing, and a way of encouraging greater reativity and innovation.

Wizards has been working diligently for more than a year to produce what we all hope will be a worthy successor to the original Star Wars CCG. I am truly sorry that you are upset with this decision. All that I can ask at this point is that you reserve final judgment until you have a chance to see the product when it launches in April.

In the meantime, while Decipher will not be producing any new Star Wars products, we expect their existing games to go on, and Decipher themselves have committed to do everything in their power to continue these games for as long as the player community wants to play them.

[[Howard Roffman]]<br />
President, Lucas Licensing
</blockquote>
<ref name="gpn-roffman" />

Wizards published the [[Star Wars Trading Card Game]] in April 2002.<ref name="icv2-2002" /> At the end of 2001 Decipher was still publishing SWCCG, [[Young Jedi]] and the [[Jedi Knights Trading Card Game]]. In a special ''[[Radio Free Decipher]]'' broadcast the same day, [[Warren Holland|Holland]] said Decipher's manufacturing and sell-off period ran through 30 April 2002.<ref name="rfd-special-0027">[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZpXfkPyurfE&t=27s Radio Free Decipher Special Broadcast (28 December, 2001): Warren Holland and the Players Committee], Player's Council, YouTube (uploaded 18 February 2022), at 00:27. Preserved copy: [https://archive.org/details/youtube-ZpXfkPyurfE Internet Archive]. Transcript: [[Radio Free Decipher/Special Broadcast (28 December 2001) transcript]].</ref> He said Decipher's offer to keep the license was more than George Lucas spent to make the original ''Star Wars'' film.<ref name="rfd-special-0347">[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZpXfkPyurfE&t=227s Radio Free Decipher Special Broadcast (28 December, 2001): Warren Holland and the Players Committee], Player's Council, YouTube (uploaded 18 February 2022), at 03:47. Preserved copy: [https://archive.org/details/youtube-ZpXfkPyurfE Internet Archive]. Transcript: [[Radio Free Decipher/Special Broadcast (28 December 2001) transcript]].</ref> It was also six times what Decipher had paid for ''Episode I''.<ref name="rfd-special-0347" /> The license agreement gave Lucasfilm a contractual right to license Decipher's game mechanics by paying royalties. Lucasfilm chose not to use that right, so any new ''Star Wars'' card game would be incompatible with Decipher's.<ref name="rfd-special-1733">[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZpXfkPyurfE&t=1053s Radio Free Decipher Special Broadcast (28 December, 2001): Warren Holland and the Players Committee], Player's Council, YouTube (uploaded 18 February 2022), at 17:33. Preserved copy: [https://archive.org/details/youtube-ZpXfkPyurfE Internet Archive]. Transcript: [[Radio Free Decipher/Special Broadcast (28 December 2001) transcript]].</ref> Lucasfilm had also turned down the virtual-card design of Decipher's planned last product, ''[[Reflections Gold]]''.<ref name="rfd-special-1923">[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZpXfkPyurfE&t=1163s Radio Free Decipher Special Broadcast (28 December, 2001): Warren Holland and the Players Committee], Player's Council, YouTube (uploaded 18 February 2022), at 19:23. Preserved copy: [https://archive.org/details/youtube-ZpXfkPyurfE Internet Archive]. Transcript: [[Radio Free Decipher/Special Broadcast (28 December 2001) transcript]].</ref> Decipher could no longer make SWCCG expansions, and cards in development were never released.<ref name="wp-swccg" /> See [[Decipher after the Star Wars license]].

== Handoff to the Players Committee ==

In January 2002 Decipher created the volunteer Players Committee to run tournaments, rulings and support for the game.<ref name="pc1" /> [[Warren Holland|Holland]] first described the committee in the 28 December 2001 broadcast: a non-profit group of volunteer players and playtesters, given email, web and office support by Decipher, which would take over prize support, the web pages, rules and FAQs and World Championship duties at the end of April 2002, and would post replacement game text for existing cards to make them tournament legal.<ref name="rfd-special-2212">[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZpXfkPyurfE&t=1332s Radio Free Decipher Special Broadcast (28 December, 2001): Warren Holland and the Players Committee], Player's Council, YouTube (uploaded 18 February 2022), at 22:12. Preserved copy: [https://archive.org/details/youtube-ZpXfkPyurfE Internet Archive]. Transcript: [[Radio Free Decipher/Special Broadcast (28 December 2001) transcript]].</ref> The Committee may issue new cards only electronically and for free, with no new film images; see [[Players Committee-Lucasfilm agreement]] and [[History of the Players Committee]].<ref name="pcabout" />
